newsitem.title: USA: Progress seen against drug-resistant bacteria.
newsitem.headline: Progress seen against drug-resistant bacteria.

text.p: A new class of experimental antibiotics may prove to be a potent weapon against bacteria that are showing dangerous resistance to standard antibiotics, scientists said Thursday.
Scientists at Merck Research Labs and Duke University Medical Center report the findings in Friday's edition of the journal Science.
Much more work has to be done in laboratory and animal studies before scientists can start testing to see whether the compounds are safe and effective in humans.

Still, the research is significant because it identifies a new target -- a lipid -- in bacteria that are resistant to antibiotics. In those bacteria, a process within the cell produces the lipid and pumps it out to form a protective oily coating on the bacteria's outer membrane.
The new class of antibiotics combats that protective process.

"That coating is necessary for the bacteria, and without it they start dying," said Dr. Christian Raetz, now the chairman of biochemistry at Duke Medical School who also worked on the drug compound while he was at Merck.
Public health experts have been increasingly anxious about antibiotic resistance that has made it harder to treat certain infections that once easily succumbed to drugs.
After shifting away from antibiotic research in the 1980s, pharmaceutical companies have renewed efforts to identify new compounds, some of which are already being tested.

The latest discovery is a Merck compound known as L-573,655 and a variant called L-161,240. It blocks one enzyme, called deacetylase, that is crucial for maintaining the structure of the outer membrane of resistant bacteria, including E. coli and some others that can cause septic shock.
Both compounds were able to cure mice infected with normally lethal doses of E. coli.
Merck labs are a divison of Merck and Co. Inc. Raetz's work at Duke has also been supported by the National Institutes of Health.
